newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-GROBBELAAR SAYS WANTED TO EXPOSE BRIBES STING.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GROBBELAAR SAYS WANTED TO EXPOSE BRIBES STING.

text.p: Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar said on Friday he had pretended to agree to rig soccer matches so he could get details of what was on offer and then report the approach to the authorities.

Grobbelaar also told a court in the city of Winchester that during the 14 years he spent with Liverpool it was common knowledge that players betted on matches they were involved in. This practice is illegal under Football Association rules.

The case against Grobbelaar is based on secretly taped conversations in which he appeared to agree to a suggestion from former business partner Chris Vincent that he rig matches for a betting syndicate.
"I wanted to know who Vincent was working with. I went along with the charade, put in stories to make it more feasible, to find out who Vincent was talking to and tell the authorities," he said.
"Had you told anybody else what you'd done?" asked prosecutor David Calvert Smith.

"No," replied Grobbelaar, who is also accused along with former Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers, ex-Wimbledon and Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim of rigging games to benefit an Asian betting syndicate.
All four deny the charges, although both keepers admit they were paid in cash by Lim for providing frequent match forecasts over the telephone.
"I suggest that match forecasting for higher rewards was canvassed and you found it hard to resist," Calvert Smith said.
"No," replied Grobbelaar in a firm voice.
One of the main accusations against Grobbelaar is that he received 40,000 pounds ($65,000) for throwing a game against Newcastle in late November of 1993.
Calvert Smith went through telephone logs which showed that Grobbelaar had called Lim just before and after the game.
"I suggest the calls to Lim must have something to do with the Newcastle-Liverpool result," the prosecutor said.
"Nothing of the sort," said the Zimbabwean.
"Why did you call Lim?" asked Calvert Smith.
"With respect, can you remember what you talked about a year ago?" asked the goalkeeper, who also said it was common knowledge that players had bet on games they were involved in.
"Some players went to the bookmakers, sometimes on the day of the game, while some gave money to friends to do it for them," he said.
"It was fairly common practice. They would put money on the first goalscorer and maybe to get a 3-1 win," he said.
"Did you players weren't supposed to bet?" asked Calvert Smith. "No," said Grobbelaar.
"I suggest that a man of your experience and intelligence must have known," retorted the prosecutor.

Earlier in the day the court watched a recording of a 3-3 draw between Liverpool and Manchester United in early January 1994. On the covert tapes Grobbelaar said he had lost 125,000 pounds reward by failing to ensure Liverpool lost.
Calvert Smith played a tape showing enthused Liverpool players applauding the crowd as they left the pitch. But Grobbelaar looked very unhappy as he walked down the tunnel.
"Is that the face of someone who's lost a lot of money?" asked Calvert Smith.
"It's the face of someone who has let in three goals against their biggest rivals," Grobbelaar replied. ($1=.6167 Pound)
